executive_summary: The defining thread running through today's content is the systematic erosion of institutional checks — legal, constitutional, and normative — under the Trump administration's exercise of power. The Justice Department's criminal inquiry into E. Jean Carroll, a private citizen who successfully sued Trump in civil court, represents a direct weaponization of federal law enforcement against a political adversary, a development that would have been unthinkable under prior administrations. The New York Times long-form analysis extends this theme into foreign policy, documenting how the Iran military action was executed without achievable objectives or constitutional oversight, a product of incompetent civilian leadership operating free from the institutional constraints designed to prevent exactly such failures. Anne Applebaum's archival piece in The Atlantic — examining why people abandon their principles — provides the intellectual framework for understanding how both developments became possible: the gradual normalization of conduct that once would have triggered institutional resistance. The Economist's finding that Trump is more unpopular than ever suggests the public is registering the cost of this institutional decay, but popularity and accountability are not the same thing, and today's news underscores how wide that gap has grown.

newsletters.title: The worst miss of all time?

items.headline: A miss for the ages
items.blurb: Wednesday at the French Open, Russia's Karen Khachanov was up match point against Marco Trungelliti of Argentina when he received the gift every player dreams of in such a big moment: a lob so feeble that they can let the ball bounce before hitting a smash. Considering the degree of difficulty, situation and by how much he missed, Khachanov immediately entered the worst-miss-of-all-time conversation. But the 30-year-old still had a match to win, and secured a 7-6(5), 5-7, 6-1, 7-6(4) win to move into the third round.

items.headline: Injuries pile up as heat continues
items.blurb: After Casper Ruud's struggle in the heat and Alexander Blockx's sprained ankle earlier in the week, the injury carnage and temperature-related issues continued Wednesday. breaking_digest.narrative:
The Justice Department has opened a criminal inquiry into E. Jean Carroll, the writer who won civil judgments against former President Donald Trump for sexual abuse and defamation, according to people familiar with the matter [1]. The inquiry marks a significant development in a legal saga that has spanned several years and resulted in substantial jury awards against Trump. No charges have been announced, and details of the inquiry's scope were not immediately available [1].

In a separate legal matter, Kenneth Iwamasa, Matthew Perry's personal assistant, was sentenced to more than three years in federal prison in connection with the actor's 2023 death from a ketamine overdose [2]. Iwamasa had pleaded guilty to charges related to his role in obtaining and administering the drug that killed the "Friends" star, making him one of several individuals prosecuted in the case [2].

longform.title: Three ways Trump is losing the war in Iran
longform.thesis: Trump's Iran war has failed strategically because incompetent civilian leadership, historical ignorance, and degraded constitutional oversight combined to produce military action without achievable objectives or a viable plan beyond initial strikes.
longform.context: Written in late May 2026 as U.S.-Iran negotiations are ongoing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end a nuclear program the administration publicly claimed it had already destroyed, the piece responds to a growing gap between the administration's triumphalist war narrative and classified intelligence assessments showing Iran retained roughly 70 percent of its missile capabilities.
arguments: The administration's public portrayal of a decisive military victory is contradicted by intelligence: Iran may retain ~70% of its missile launchers and prewar stocks, 30 of 33 missile sites along the Strait of Hormuz remain intact, and the U.S. depleted a substantial share of its own missile stocks to destroy a small fraction of Iranian capability — while Iran damaged or destroyed at least 42 American aircraft and inflicted significant damage on U.S. regional bases.

Trump's strategic failure stems from a fundamental misreading of Iran as analogous to Venezuela — a corrupt, pliable regime — when Iran is a theocratic state that survived hundreds of thousands of casualties in the Iran-Iraq war, endured decades of sanctions and sabotage, and whose population includes people 'willing to die for their beliefs'; this produced a Plan A (decapitation strike) with no viable Plan B when Iran did not collapse.

Eliot Cohen's framing of 'Lions Led by Donkeys' captures the core dysfunction: competent military execution was undermined by incompetent and corrupt civilian leadership, illustrating why Trump was, in the author's words, 'never an acceptable choice for president' as commander in chief — a structural problem extending beyond Trump alone to the broader breakdown of civilian oversight and institutional checks on executive war-making.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it documents, while a war is still active, how the gap between public war narrative and classified reality is shaping failed negotiations — the U.S. is bargaining to reopen a strait it said would be open and to end a nuclear program it said it obliterated. It also advances a broader argument that the Iran war's failure is not an anomaly but a predictable consequence of electing someone temperamentally and intellectually unfit for wartime command. The piece implicitly warns that Iran's post-war position — with theoretical Hormuz control now actualized — may be stronger than its prewar position, a strategic reversal with lasting regional consequences.
questions_raised: The article is truncated and never fully develops the 'history and civics' explanations beyond the leadership failure — leaving unresolved what specific institutional or constitutional breakdowns enabled this strategic miscalculation to go unchecked.

If Iran has retained the bulk of its missile arsenal and now exercises actual rather than theoretical control of the Strait of Hormuz, the piece raises but does not answer whether any negotiated settlement can restore the prewar strategic balance, or whether the war has permanently shifted leverage toward Tehran.
